title: Minimum Speed to Arrive on Time
statement:
You must reach the office within `hour` hours, and the trip is `n` train rides taken in order: ride `i` covers `dist[i]` kilometres. Every train runs at the same speed, which must be a positive integer number of kilometres per hour.

A train may only leave at a whole hour (0, 1, 2, ...). When a ride ends between whole hours you wait for the next whole hour before the following ride; nothing happens after the last ride, so its time counts exactly.

Return the smallest speed that gets you to the office at or before time `hour`, or `-1` if no speed is fast enough. `hour` has at most two digits after the decimal point, and whenever an answer exists it is at most `10^7`.
constraints: hour has at most two digits after the decimal point
The answer, when it exists, is at most 10^7
notes:
## Intuition

Faster trains never make you later, so "speed `s` is on time" is false for small speeds and true from some point on. Instead of trying speeds one by one (up to `10^7` of them), binary search for the first speed that works; each guess is checked by adding up the ride times.

At any speed, the first `n - 1` rides each end on a whole hour after rounding up, so they take at least `n - 1` hours, and the last ride takes a positive amount of time. If `hour <= n - 1`, no speed helps.

## Approach

1. Turn `hour` into whole hundredths, `limit`, so all comparisons are exact integers.
2. If `limit <= (n - 1) * 100`, return `-1`.
3. `canArrive(speed)`: add `ceil(dist[i] / speed)` for every ride but the last into `whole`; the time left over is `spare = limit - whole * 100` hundredths, and the last ride fits when `100 * dist[n - 1] <= speed * spare`.
4. Binary search `left = 1`, `right = 10^7`: if `mid` works, the answer is `mid` or smaller (`right = mid`); otherwise it is larger (`left = mid + 1`).
5. When `left == right`, that is the smallest working speed.

## Example 1, step by step

`dist = [1, 3, 2]`, `hour = 6`, so `limit = 600`, more than `200`. Every speed checked from `mid = 5000000` downward still works, because `whole` stays small; the search keeps shrinking `right` until `mid = 1`: `whole = 1 + 3 = 4`, `spare = 200`, and `100 * 2 = 200 <= 1 * 200`, so speed `1` works and the answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log 10^7): about 24 checks, each a pass over `dist`.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Do not round up the last ride; you arrive the moment it ends.
- Comparing `whole + dist[n - 1] / speed <= hour` in floating point can be off by a hair when the arrival is exactly `hour` (for example `1 + 16 / 25` versus `1.64`); hundredths avoid that.
- Without the `-1` check first, the search would return `10^7` for an impossible trip.
- Arriving exactly at `hour` counts as on time, so the test is `<=`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of rides |
| `limit` | `hour` in hundredths of an hour |
| `whole` | whole hours spent on all rides but the last |
| `spare` | hundredths of an hour left for the last ride |
| `left`, `right` | the range that still contains the answer |
| `mid` | the speed being tested |
